report:
## Report

The evidence suggests your assumption is likely incorrect—olive leaf extract (OLE) shows modest but real blood-pressure-lowering effects, though the evidence base is still limited.

Several human randomized controlled trials support an antihypertensive effect. A well-cited 2011 double-blind, active-controlled RCT in stage-1 hypertension patients found that OLE (500 mg twice daily) produced systolic/diastolic blood pressure reductions comparable to the prescription ACE-inhibitor captopril (12.5–25 mg twice daily) over 8 weeks (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/). A separate randomized, double-blind, crossover trial in adults with mildly elevated blood pressure found that a phenolic-rich OLE significantly reduced blood pressure and improved several cardiovascular markers compared with placebo (link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-016-1188-y). A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane) examining OLE's effects on cardiovascular risk factors, including blood pressure, found supportive—though not uniformly conclusive—evidence across pooled trials (link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13098-022-00920-y).

Important caveats: most trials are small, short-term, and industry- or manufacturer-linked (e.g., specific standardized extracts like EFLA®943), and effect sizes vary by dose, oleuropein content, and baseline blood pressure. Effects appear more consistent in people with elevated or stage-1 hypertension than in normotensive individuals, and OLE should not be considered a replacement for standard antihypertensive therapy.

**Conclusion:** Based on multiple RCTs and a meta-analysis, olive leaf extract does appear to modestly reduce blood pressure in hypertensive/pre-hypertensive adults—contrary to a flat "no."
